```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = F)
```

```{r}
# Core libraries for modeling and visualization
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)   # Penguin dataset
library(rpart)            # Decision trees
library(rpart.plot)       # Tree visualization
library(randomForest)     # Random forests
library(gbm)              # Gradient boosting
library(pdp)              # Partial dependence plots
library(vip)              # Variable importance

```

## Modeling with several ML approaches

We split the data into training and test data sets.
```{r}
# Clean data (remove missing values)
df <- penguins |> drop_na()

# Set seed for reproducibility (critical for ML!)
set.seed(1)

# 80/20 split: train on 80%, evaluate on unseen 20%
idx <- sample.int(nrow(df), size = floor(0.8 * nrow(df)))
train <- df[idx, ]
test  <- df[-idx, ]

# Verify split sizes
cat("Training observations:", nrow(train), "\n")
cat("Test observations:", nrow(test), "\n")
```
We split data as Models can "memorize" training ̥
data (overfitting). The test set simulates future unseen penguins—only test performance reflects real-world accuracy.

## Linear Model(lm)
It is the Simplest approach it assumes straight-line relationships between predictors and body mass.
```{r}
# Fit model using ALL predictors (".") except response (body_mass_g)
model_lm <- train |> lm(body_mass_g ~., data =_) # "~." means that the equation uses all the other variables but the response variable (in this case body mass) 
summary(model_lm)
view(df)

```
### Decision Tree
Non-linear approach, it splits data into homogeneous groups
```{r}
# First: default tree (may be too simple)
model_dt <- train |> rpart(body_mass_g~., data=_)
rpart.plot(model_dt)

# Second: deeper tree (lower cp = more splits allowed)
model_dt <- train |> 
  rpart(body_mass_g~., data=_, control=rpart.control(cp = 0.001))
rpart.plot(model_dt)
# Cross-validation table: shows optimal complexity
printcp(model_dt)


```
### random forest
Ensemble method it averages predictions from 500 decorrelated trees, it reduces overfitting.
```{r}
model_rf <- train |> 
  randomForest(body_mass_g~.,data=_)
model_rf
```
### gradient boosting
Sequential learning, each new tree corrects errors from previous trees
```{r}
# Default settings (500 trees, depth=1)
model_gb <- train |> 
  gbm(body_mass_g~.,data=_)
model_gb
```

## Model Assessment and Comparison
Evaluate ALL models on the SAME unseen test data.
We now use the test dataset for the comparing model performance:
```{r}
# Generate predictions
predicted_lm <- predict(model_lm, test)
predicted_dt <- predict(model_dt, test)
predicted_rf <- predict(model_rf, test)
predicted_gb <- predict(model_gb, test) # Use 100 trees 
# Helper function for consistent plots
# Show all four models
plot(predicted_lm, test$body_mass_g)
plot(predicted_dt, test$body_mass_g)
plot(predicted_rf, test$body_mass_g)
plot(predicted_gb, test$body_mass_g)

# Calculate R² on TEST data (not training!)
r2_lm <- cor(predicted_lm, test$body_mass_g)^2
r2_dt <- cor(predicted_dt, test$body_mass_g)^2
r2_rf <- cor(predicted_rf, test$body_mass_g)^2
r2_gb <- cor(predicted_gb, test$body_mass_g)^2

# Create comparison table
performance <- tibble(
  Model = c("Linear Model", "Decision Tree", "Random Forest", "Gradient Boosting"),
  Test_R2 = c(r2_lm, r2_dt, r2_rf, r2_gb)
) |> arrange(desc(Test_R2))

knitr::kable(performance, digits = 3, caption = "Test Set R² (Higher = Better)")

```
Note:Training R² is always higher than test R² (optimistic bias), Random Forest typically wins for tabular data like this Decision trees often underperform due to high variance

## Model Interpretation

vip: variable importance plot, showing the relative importance of predictor variables (which factors are important to predict body mass?)

```{r}
# Linear model importance (absolute coefficient size)
vip(model_lm, num_features = 6, bar = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Linear Model: Predictor Importance") +
  theme_minimal()

# Random forest importance (built-in metric)
varImpPlot(model_rf, main = "Random Forest: Predictor Importance")
```

pdp: partial dependence plot, showing how X is related to Y (such as flipper length and body mass)

```{r}
# Linear model relationship
pdp_lm <- model_lm |> partial("flipper_length_mm", train = train)
autoplot(pdp_lm) +
  labs(title = "Linear Model: Flipper Length Effect", 
       subtitle = "Holding other variables constant") +
  theme_minimal()

# Random forest relationship (with individual observation paths)
pdp_rf <- model_rf |> partial("flipper_length_mm", train = train, ice = TRUE)
autoplot(pdp_rf) +
  labs(title = "Random Forest: Flipper Length Effect",
       subtitle = "Gray lines = individual penguins; Black = average") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Main point to remember: Always split data before modeling—test set is the only honest evaluator. Training metrics lie test performance reveals true accuracy. Flipper length dominates penguin mass prediction (biologically meaningful). Random Forest is robust default it handles non-linearity without tuning. Interpretability ≠ accuracy tradeoff, the Linear models explain why; forests predict what.
